Chapter Four: The Division of the World and the Logic of Imperialism
Picture this: as finance capital and giant monopolies stretched their influence further and further, the whole world became a prize—a target for division and re-division among just a handful of the most powerful capitalist countries.
But here’s the thing: this wasn’t about random land grabs or isolated power plays. It was actually a built-in feature of advanced capitalism itself. At this stage, the globe gets carved up by those few who hold the most power.
If you look back at earlier times, colonial expansion was all about chasing new lands, resources, maybe even a shortcut to the spice trade. But by the time monopoly capitalism took hold, everything had changed. Most of the world had already been explored—claimed, even. Now, the question was how to control, reorganize, and squeeze more out of these territories.
So, how did this division of the world actually play out? Well, it took a few different forms:
Sometimes, it meant direct colonial rule—one powerful nation stamping its authority over another land and its people.
Other times, it was all about economic domination—using investments, trade deals, and financial muscle to call the shots, instead of sending in the troops.
And then there were those so-called “spheres of influence”—essentially, the big players would agree, at least for the moment, to let each other keep their spoils, as long as nobody crossed certain lines.
But let’s be clear: this carving up of the world wasn’t some tidy, peaceful process. It was fierce, full of rivalry and backroom deals, with alliances that shifted as quickly as the winds. And when those interests clashed, violence was never far behind.
As each power scrambled for a bigger slice of the pie—competing for colonies, markets, and resources—conflict became almost unavoidable. These tensions often exploded into outright war.
But you know, this wasn’t just about grabbing land. It was about control—over resources, over labor, over the very flow of money around the globe. The strongest nations used everything they had—economic pull, military force—to shape entire regions, and it was almost always at the expense of those who lived there.
Think of the logic of imperialism like a high-stakes game of musical chairs. Each major power is desperate to grab a seat before the music stops. Only, in this case, the stakes weren’t just bruised knees—they were the wealth of nations, the fate of millions, and the future of the world order.
Let’s look at a few key things to remember here:
By the early twentieth century, the world was almost completely divided among just a few big powers.
They used both direct rule and more subtle economic tools to keep control—sometimes with armies, sometimes just with contracts and investments.
The threat of conflict was always hanging overhead, as these powers tried to defend, or even expand, their interests.
And through it all, global inequality got worse—riches and resources flowed from the far corners of the world straight into the hands of those at the center.
Here’s what all this really means: this stage of imperialism isn’t just a passing phase, or the result of a few bad decisions. It’s the logical outcome of how monopoly capitalism and finance capital evolve. The drive to divide—and control—the world is baked right into the system itself.
